new_d.text: The view that “every event is necessitated by antecedent events and conditions together with the laws of nature”.

new_text.text: Carl Hoefer's working definition is that, given a specified way things are at a time, “the way things go thereafter is fixed as a matter of natural law”.

He frames the thesis for the whole state of the world, since ordinary ideas of events have no correlate in any modern physical theory, and he reports John Earman's quip that defining determinism through causation explains a vague concept in terms of “a truly obscure one”.
Laplace imagined “An intelligence knowing all the forces acting in nature at a given instant”, to which the whole future would be open, and Hoefer notes that Laplace probably had God in mind.
Spinoza holds that “Nothing in the universe is contingent, but all things are conditioned to exist and operate in a particular manner by the necessity of the divine nature”.

Determinism and predictability come apart: sensitive dependence on initial conditions can make prediction impossible for finite agents even in a deterministic world, although Karl Popper defined determinism in terms of predictability.

Fatalism holds that events are destined to occur no matter what we do, with the guarantee lying in the will of the gods, divine foreknowledge or some teleological aspect of the universe, and Hoefer treats it as separable from determinism by natural law to the extent that these can be disentangled from natural law.

Even classical mechanics leaves room for indeterminism: on John Norton's dome a resting ball may start to slide with no violation of Newton's laws, and Hoefer describes the “space invader”, the time-reverse of a body that escapes to infinity, an escape Xia showed five bodies can bring about by gravitation alone.

In quantum mechanics the evolution of a wavefunction under the Schrödinger equation is normally taken to be deterministic; the more common twentieth-century approach adds a collapse of the wavefunction at measurement, Everettian readings keep the deterministic evolution throughout, and David Bohm's theory of 1952 is deterministic.

On free will, a long tradition of compatibilists holds that freedom is fully compatible with determinism, incompatibilists deny it, and Hume argued that determinism, or at least some causality principle along the lines of “same cause, same effect”, is a necessary condition of freedom.
Hoefer calls John Earman's A Primer on Determinism (1986) “the richest storehouse of information on the truth or falsity of determinism in various physical theories”.

determinism.s: Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814); Spinoza, Ethics I, Prop. 29 (Elwes trans.)

new_d.text: The view that “there are significant ways in which our concepts and knowledge are gained independently of sense experience”.

new_text.text: The Stanford Encyclopedia sets out three theses, at least one of which a rationalist adopts: that some truths are knowable by intuition alone and others by deduction from them, that we have knowledge of some truths as part of our nature, and that we have some concepts as part of our rational nature.
It groups Descartes, Spinoza and Leibniz as the Continental Rationalists, and cautions that such labels can oversimplify their views.
Leibniz's New Essays argues that necessary truths, such as those of pure mathematics, must have principles whose proof does not depend on instances.
Spinoza sets out his Ethics in geometrical order, from definitions and axioms to propositions and their proofs.
Kant, who first applied the distinction between rationalists and empiricists, held that a priori knowledge of things in themselves, the claim of transcendent metaphysics, is impossible.

rationalism.s: Descartes, Meditations on First Philosophy (1641); Spinoza, Ethics (1677); Leibniz, New Essays on Human Understanding (written 1704)

new_d.text: Aristotle's four kinds of cause: material (what a thing is made of), formal (its form), efficient (what brought it about) and final (what it is for).

new_text.text: The Greek word is aitia, and Andrea Falcon suggests that “it can be useful to think of a cause as a certain type of explanation”.
Aristotle gives his general account of the four causes in Physics II 3 and Metaphysics V 2.
In the making of a bronze statue, the bronze enters the explanation as the material cause, and the statue enters the explanation of each step of the work as the final cause.
In nature, Aristotle observes, “the form and the end often coincide, and they are formally the same as that which produces the change”.
Hobbes and Descartes took William Harvey's work as a turn away from Galenic and Aristotelian anatomy, with its appeal to final causes, toward mechanistic science.

new_d.text: Aristotle's dunamis and energeia: a capacity to be or do something, and its realization. The acorn is potentially an oak; the grown oak is the actuality toward which it develops.

new_text.text: In the strictest sense, C. D. C. Reeve writes, “a dunamis is the power that a thing has to produce a change”.
Metaphysics IX (Theta) argues that actuality is prior to potentiality in account, in time and in substance.

Because what is potentially may possibly not be, eternal movement needs a starting-point “the very substance of which is activity”, and “the primary essence does not have matter, since it is an actuality”.

new_d.text: What a thing is, as its definition states it.

new_text.text: “Essence” is the standard English translation of Aristotle's phrase to ti ên einai; for Aristotle there is an essence only of those things whose account is a definition, and each substance is one and the same as its essence.

Ibn Sīnā argued that essence and existence are distinct, since, as Fedor Benevich puts his argument, “we can know what things are (human beings, horses, triangles) without knowing whether they exist”.
Locke separates the real essence of a material thing, its atomic constitution, which is “quite unknown to us”, from its nominal essence, the general idea by which we pick out a sort.
Sartre's existentialism reverses the order for human beings: existence precedes essence, meaning that a human being “exists, turns up, appears on the scene, and, only afterwards, defines himself”.

essence.s: Aristotle, Metaphysics VII.4–6; Locke, Essay III.iii; Sartre, Existentialism Is a Humanism (1946)

The Stoics held virtue alone suffices; the Epicureans identified it with tranquility and freedom from pain.

new_d.text: Aristotle's term for the highest human good, usually translated “happiness” or “flourishing”: activity of the rational part of the soul in accordance with virtue.

new_text.text: In F. H. Peters's translation the good of man is “exercise of his faculties in accordance with excellence or virtue, or, if there be more than one, in accordance with the best and most complete virtue”.
Richard Kraut writes that “using reason well over the course of a full life is what happiness consists in”, and that one must also possess “such goods as friends, wealth, and power”.
In Book X perfect happiness consists in contemplation, and the happiest kind of life is that of a philosopher.
